utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Before we continue with the examination of the witness, I will say something very briefly about the matter which was raised late yesterday afternoon. The premise for counsel's remarks that the question asked was based on the witness summary is wrong. Whether the question has a proper basis in the evidence is not something which need detain us at this time, at this stage of the trial, and it is trite that the summary is not evidence. I would, however, wish to emphasise the right and indeed the duty of the Chamber to ask questions in these proceedings which, although of a fundamentally adversarial character, also have significant inquisitorial elements. Continue, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. Rodic will continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness G. Let us continue with the examination. Can you tell us something more about the lighting in the Keraterm compound? The lampposts that we saw on the photograph there, did they work? Rather, did they provide lights in Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: When there was power, then, yes, they did light the compound, but when there was no electricity, then we didn't have any lights either. One could see it from the town. If the town was dark, we were in darkness too, and when the town had electricity, then we also had it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And the lighting came from those lampposts in front of Rooms 3 and 4 in the grass?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember exactly where they were. I only know that when there was electricity, then we also had lights, but if the town was in darkness, then Keraterm was in darkness too.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know where was bread brought for prisoners was kept?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. I only know when it was distributed. I had nothing to do with them but I know when the food was distributed, that was sometime between 3.00 and 6.00, and I know that the queue would be formed in front of a room next to Room 2 where the food was distributed, but where it was kept, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell us, do you know who distributed that food?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know there was a female who usually did it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What was the situation with the water supply in Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Water supply, that was -- it was very bad. At times there was very little water; at times there was no water at all. When I moved over to Room 4, it improved slightly because there was a hydrant right there, so that if there was no other water, we could get it from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: But does it mean that there was some water shortages, same as electricity at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot really tell you if there were shortages or not. I do not know what the situation was. At times there was water; at times there wasn't. While I was in Room 2, they would let us out sometimes, and we would have some plastic bottles and fill them. At times you have water; at times somebody gives it to you; at times you don't. I mean, that is how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the water was also brought in water trucks to the compound?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: On various occasions, I did see that, yes, not very often. But there were a few occasions when water was brought by trucks to the compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell us, of course, if you know, with regard to the medical aid, was that organised in some situations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was organised. How many times, I don't know. Once or twice perhaps following the massacre in Room 3. I know after that, they took away people. And before that, the guy had a arm broken. One or two also were taken to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And tell me, as for the organisation of shift work, do you know something about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, this. Well, I wasn't in a situation where I could know anything about it. I only know when which shift was, but to say something about the organisation, I do not know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: But the working hours, the changes, when did they change?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that shift changes took place in the morning and in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And tell me, did the guards whom were part of the security service of Keraterm have their posts, have their fixed posts where they stood guard or did they move around Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, most of the time they moved freely around Keraterm, that is, within the compound, which was fenced in.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So there were not strictly fixed sentry posts where shifts took place and where they were all the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, where you entered, where that hut was, I think that is where shift changes took place and where they spent most of the time, but they mostly walked around the camp. At times they would come to our rooms, talk with people, because they also had friends amongst us.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And tell me, was there a guard at the gate, at the entrance into Keraterm, that is, before the scales, before the weigh hut, by the moving gate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. I know where that is, but I cannot really tell you. At times there would be somebody there, at times there wouldn't. And there was this hut with the scales, so at times there was somebody in it, at times there was somebody outside it. It is difficult to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I do not insist. I am simply trying to either prompt your memory or see what you remember. Tell me, did you know Kajin's brother?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Then you do not know if he worked in the camp too?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only heard about it, but I didn't know that, that there was -- I knew that there was Kajin and his brother, but I did not know him. I simply couldn't recognise him. I didn't know who that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You said that when you arrived, Kajin was mentioned to you by other prisoners; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You also said that Kajin was there to prevent beating and ill-treatment of prisoners.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that happened in my presence. I could see that, and I can testify about that, but Zigic beat us nevertheless.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And did other prisoners tell you that there were some other similar situations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I suppose there were other similar situations. He could lock us and, nevertheless, what happened happened, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: No, I'm asking about similar situations that one or some of the prisoners may have mentioned Kajin putting an end to beating or something.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot really tell you. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you this because when the Prosecutor asked you how did you know that Kajin was a shift commander, you said, "People said that he was a commander and he would come, and if something happened, he would put an end to that and that is how we knew that he was a shift commander."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I am sorry about what happened to you personally, but I must ask you this because it is related to the event when you were beaten. So could you please tell me, when you told us about 22 prisoners being beaten, you were one of them. Is it correct to say that Zigic called out Kozaracians from the room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. It was Zigic and Duca Knezevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me how many other people took part in the beating? Roughly.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was beaten by Zigic himself and another guy who, as I told you, never said anything. He was only there and executed a detail, performed all sorts of sordid tasks, and to this I understood Duca and others, who were -- who were there, who were present there but did not take part in the beating.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Were there some soldiers there too?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean in that line where we were, on our side?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. I mean among those who beat you or watched you being beaten?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was Zigic who beat and that other guy, and there was Knezevic and Banovics and others. Two or three others were there standing by, but you are just thinking how to stay alive. You don't really think about such things. I can only tell you who was with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is it true that it happened in the afternoon, or rather towards the -- sometimes at twilight, at dusk, when guards -- at the time when guards usually change?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think it was in the afternoon, but at what time in the afternoon, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me something more about when you were told to line up and face one another in those lines? How was this line placed in relation Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25 to Rooms 1 and 2?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: The line was -- well, you have rooms which are 1, 2, 3, 4, so the line was roughly about in the same position, that is from the Prijedor-Banja Luka road, that is where the first two men stood and we then were towards Kozara, northward. That is how the lines went.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In other words, we can say that these two lines ran parallel with the building, is it? They were lines in parallel with the building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the building and this is how we stood.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you remember where you were, nearer the road or the opposite side?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. I was the last one in the direction of Kozara. Redzo Grabic faced me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So you were the last one toward Kozara, from the road and then the last one in that column. And where did you face, Redzo and --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I faced Redzo and the town, Prijedor, or the petrol station, if you like, and Redzo faced Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Which means that you had Room 4 in front of you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no in my case, Rooms 1 and 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So you had Room 2 in front of you, or rather between you and the room was Redzo Grabic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And the blow that was dealt you at the back of your head with a metal rod, it was a powerful blow, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was. It all went black. And a few minutes later, I realised that I would faint and went -- when they let us go, I fainted and --

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. I will ask about it later. What I'm asking now is that particular blow. You told us that you were hit, and when they hit you on the back, that another one then hits you from the front, and that you have a scar. That is, you were hit a second time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was hit with the boot. I was kicked with a boot here below the chin, and my flesh was cut here.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You described the situation, that it all went black before your eyes. Were you frightened at that moment? Did you fear for your life?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Come on, I mean, who wouldn't? Of course I was frightened. Who wouldn't be frightened?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that, but I have to ask you that. Please understand. And under those circumstances which you describe, did you dare react somehow or resist Zigic so that he would stop beating you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't -- did not dare do anything because you have to keep silent and just wait to see what next would happen to you. Otherwise, you would -- it would be even worse.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And isn't it true that when then Kajin came from the entrance by the weigh bridge, that he then said to stop that and to let you go into your rooms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I apologise, something is missing from the transcript. Let me repeat this question. So is it correct to say that when Kajin came from the direction of the entrance into Keraterm and the scales, and said to stop it and to move into rooms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And in your view, did Kajin save you on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, listen, I suppose he did, but he also could have locked that room so that nobody could get to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me if anybody else asked from you money and valuables before Goran Grahovac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was nobody before him. He was the first one who came and requested money and gold.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: When you described that situation, you said that there was Fustar together with Grahovac and that when they saw the new guard commander, that Grahovac escaped across the Keraterm fence; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me where was Fustar at that point?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fustar, we, that is all three of us, were next to the wall, next to the wall of that weigh hut, to the north. Grahovac was sitting on a beer crate, and I stood next to him, and Fustar was to Grahovac's left. So Grahovac was in the middle, I was to the left, and Fustar was to his right, perhaps a metre, not more than two metres away from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What I want to know, what I would like you to tell us, if you know, when Grahovac fled, did Fustar stay there or did he go somewhere?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that point, Fustar saw the commander first because he was on the corner with me and he said, "Beat it or scram. Here comes the commander." So he allowed me to run to the room, and Grahovac escaped across the fence. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And were there any guards in the direction which Grahovac took when he fled?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say that because at that moment, I also had to run towards the rooms so that I turned my back on him.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I ask you this because I wanted to know if you know if anybody tried to prevent him from escaping. Is it true that you said that Zigic came to the camp as he pleased, that he did as he pleased, and that nobody could do anything about it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right. That is true. He came to the camp as he pleased, he did as he pleased.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can that also be said of a man called Duca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were always together, Duca and Zigic. One could say that on in -- 90 per cent of the cases when they came to Keraterm, they came together.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Does that also hold true of brothers Banovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were there often, but I believe that they were both on the same shift, even though I can't affirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And tell me, to your knowledge, did any of the prisoners in Keraterm ever report his beating to somebody?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you that. I do not know that. But if you told some -- as a rule, if you told somebody that you had been beaten, you more often than not ended up on the garbage dump outside. You could not really tell anyone that you had been beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Which means that there was the danger of revenge.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a danger. If a soldier stops you and says, "What's the matter? Is your arm broken," or, "You have injuries on your face or your head, what happened to you?" and you answer, "I fell off the stairs," or, "I stumbled or something," that is what we did as a rule, because if someone said that he'd been hit by a soldier, in 90 per cent of the cases, we could know that that man would be killed. And when you saw that, nobody dared say any more about what had happened to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Could one say then that under the circumstances, there was no authority and officer in Keraterm who would then punish those who did those things to prisoners, who would take disciplinary measures, remove those people from work there? Was there anything of the kind at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: In some cases, yes. In my own case, when Zigic did that, well, Kajin evidently was the authority which stopped that. But there were also a number of cases. At the gate, there was a soldier. He could always prevent anyone from entering the camp if he was not a member there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand the situation, and you also told us about it. You said that there were a number of beatings, that it was done by people who came from outside, that at times guards also -- Keraterm guards participated in all this, and that is why I'm asking you, because of -- was there any superior, somebody who was senior, somebody with authority who could tell the guard to stop, to get away, to dismiss him from work or something?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot really give you an answer to this. Maybe there was, maybe there wasn't. I was just a prisoner there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And tell me, in this group for special treatment that you mentioned, those -- the men in that group, you said that you were -- that they were also beaten whilst in the room. Can you tell us exactly who entered and who did it in the room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were put right next to the door, left of the door. Zigic and Knezevic entered the room, but other guys came in too. I know the two of them only too well, because they were always the first to take everybody out and all the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, in the light of your own experience, you were at Trnopolje, you were in the military police barracks, you were at Keraterm, in certain situations you have experienced first hand and you saw other situations, the entire situation at Prijedor, would you call -- call all of this a chaotic situation, given that certain individuals were doing whatever they wanted?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the one hand it may have been chaotic. On the other hand, not really, because if we -- if all of us who were Muslim were arrested, that means that once it had power and did what they wanted. Now, what the real situation was, I don't know. I'm not a military strategist or anything like that, so I couldn't tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I agree with you that one side detained the other, but when I referred to the chaotic situation, I was referring to the absence of order and discipline, conducting things in an orderly manner, because you yourself mentioned all the beatings and the taking of valuables away and things like that. So that was in reference to that that I asked whether it was a chaotic situation.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be really, really hard for me to explain to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Let me try to assist you. Let me try to assist you. You said that you served in the JNA. At that time, it was nearly two years, if I'm Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25 not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was 18 months about.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: After that, were you ever a member of the reserve?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was, on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In respect of organisation, subordination, and then punishing and censuring of the subordinates by the superiors, in light of that, was that the experience that you had when you served in the military?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was a completely different situation. When you were issued an order, you had to do what you were told, whereas here, everybody did whatever they pleased or wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have completed my questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Rodic. Mr. Vucicevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, I'm Dusan Vucicevic, attorney from Chicago, and I represent Dragan Kolundzija. You gave a statement to the investigators of this Tribunal on 11 November 1995; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date, but it was 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: 11 November. And on that location, when you concluded with your statement, the gentleman from the Prosecution had either read back to you the statement or given it to you to read?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He said that it should be read. And there was a lady who was an interpreter. However, she was unable to say everything. She was an ethnic Slovene, so she -- I had to explain certain words to her.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, the Office of the Prosecutor did not provide an interpreter who could understand you fully?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the other way around. So there were some corrections.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: So the corrections of this interview were done in a way that eventually you signed the document of your own will?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After all the corrections, I did sign the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: When did the corrections take place after you signed the statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: The corrections were entered last year.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: But let me point -- let me put it to you that in the document that you signed on 11 November, 1995, there were no corrections made. What I would like to do -- this is the document signed by you on 11 November, 1995. Could you please review it and say what you had corrected before signing it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember, for instance, that from the village where I lived, 2.000 to 3.000 of us left. That is not correct. I couldn't have said that because I know that there were 11 homes and about 100 people and there were Grozdanics, and that was about ten homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: I don't want to go that wide. What I'm interested in, did you correct anything with respect to the shooting that occurred at Room 3, that is, that single paragraph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to review it. It was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. When this incident took place, you were in Room 4?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: How far were you from the door?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Somewhere between three and four metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Were you on a pallet or styrofoam or on a blanket?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had a pallet and we had neither styrofoam or a blanket.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: But some of the detainees had styrofoam?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my room, no one did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: How far were you from the wall, the partition wall between Rooms 3 and 4?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was again three or up to four metres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, had you fallen asleep that night after the door was closed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who would have -- who could have slept when there was shooting all night long?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear noise, voices, and some kind of banging coming from the prisoners in Room 4 because you were so close?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: First I heard moans and cries, and then there was noise and banging on the door because people just got crazed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: I see that you gave a statement to the OTP on 11 November 1995, and in it you said: [In English] "They ran out of oxygen so they pulled themselves up to try to open the windows." Did anybody tell you that or you heard them talking about that, about that action, climbing up to open the windows?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I heard that but before that --

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: You heard the inmates from Room 3 because there was only a thin wall between you. You heard them when they were talking about climbing to open the windows, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not hear that. People were jumping up to open the window. They were trying to smash the window.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the windows, and you heard the jumping and noise coming from Room number 3?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: You said they ran out of oxygen. You meant to say they ran out of air, they couldn't breathe; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Were they asking that the door be open or the windows be open while they were running out of air? They were yelling and screaming asking for that, weren't they? You were right there. You could hear it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: And since you were so close to that room and you were awake all night long, you didn't hear a bomb being thrown into the Room number 3, explosion of a bomb in Room 3? Could you hear that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: A bomb could have been heard but I did not hear any bomb, any explosions. It was just rifles and machine-guns.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Since you were so close, you didn't smell any plain natural gas or any other poison gas in your room? Did you smell it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Cannot answer that question. I don't recall it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: As far as you remember, you couldn't smell anything unusual?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Listen, the smells, we had a barrel there where we urinated, and of course it was closed and it was very hot during that period, so that was the --

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... ammonia and from the -- I'll repeat the question because it's not on the record. Of course there was a stench from ammonia that you had from the barrel that you had in your room, but you didn't feel any other type of the noxious smells?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't recall having smelled anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: You testified to the OTP in November of 1995 that truck -- "A truckload of soldiers came around 2100 hours and took about 30 people from Room 3. After about a half an hour, there were gunshots. Among those 30 people were a number of brothers." That was three years after the incident had happened. Could you see these soldiers coming in at -- and remember it correctly at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not remember the exact time. I said that that was the lunch, that is after dinner that we had, but we saw the soldiers when we were coming back because they had arrived at a gate in trucks. After that, we were all put in rooms.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... you said to the Prosecutor. Now it's nine years later, and the Prosecutor said all that you know about that incident is what you heard from others. So I'm only asking what did you remember then, and what is your recollection, not what you heard from the others because that was -- the side that is presenting you as a witness already has put it as a part of your testimony, that is you are unsure about.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw exactly when the soldiers arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: How many machine-guns were there in the camp when you were brought in on the first day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that there were one or two. I don't know exactly. As you put it, after nine and a half years, it's hard to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: So when you said there were three guns that had been firing in the direction of Room 3, you're not sure about that either? You didn't see it, did you? You couldn't see it, because you said the door was closed.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: A day before, a desk was placed, with sandbags, and one machine-gun was placed. This was before the massacre, three or four or five days.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: So as you remember now after nine years, that was set up two days before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say two days. I said two or three. Several days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Vucicevic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Actually, Your Honour, the witness said, "Three or four or five days."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: I do -- appreciate it. Thank you. Thank you, Ms. Baly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: You have testified also in Omarska trial, and I'm going to read something that you have said there just to refresh your memory, and I'll ask you a couple of questions from the same subject. The question was: [As read]

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned some of the individuals at the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25 checkpoints were wearing fur caps, caps with a cockade on it. What did that indicate to you? What did that mean to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it meant to me they were Chetniks because there was a lot of talk about them, and one knows them from history.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: And you -- how did you or why was it that you correlated someone wearing that type of cap with a cockade on it to identify them as Chetnik? Why was it that you would make that association?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a feeling I had. I simply knew that. Quite a number of films had been made in Yugoslavia about this, and I also worked for a film, "The Battle on the ..." And that wasn't finished. Could you tell this Court what -- could you please tell this Court what was the name of that film that you worked on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: The film was called, "Battle of Neretva," and the second was, "Battle of Kozara," and the third one was called, "Gorge." Those were the three films.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: What was your -- what was the extent of your participation in those movies -- those films. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the filming of the "Battle of Neretva," I was a soldier, and I was involved for seven months. One day I was wearing a black -- black clothing and a fur hat with a cockade. On another day of shooting, I was wearing a partisan uniform with a five-pointed star. And as the needs changed, this is how we -- what we put on as costumes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: And how long approximately have you participated in filming of "Battle on Neretva"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I participated between six and seven months.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: And how long was your military service, length of your military service at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Eighteen months.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what was the extent of your participation in that movie about Kozara?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, in the fourth or fifth grade and -- so the school -- we went there with the school, and we participated in the filming as children.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... you could remember what kind of a costume --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Vucicevic, I'm waiting to see the relevance of the witness' thespian qualities to these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll just repeat my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What do his acting abilities have to do with these proceedings? Tell me.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, here we go. Yesterday, when the Prosecutor asked the question: [As read]

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: And you also said on that occasion that Kajin said that he disagreed with the Chetnik policy.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That he disagreed with the Chetnik policy, with the SDS policy, that he really ... That was the answer.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: ... that he really did not want to see people tortured and mistreated. If somebody was guilty, they should be brought to justice ... And on and on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Vucicevic, don't make a speech. And I should -- I'm just reminded to tell you that the interpreters are having difficulties with translating. You are speaking too fast, and you're also overlapping. Now, just tell me very briefly, what is the relevance of this testimony?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: The witness has testified about the two kinds of soldiers on the checkpoints. There was JNA soldiers or Serbian soldiers and other soldiers that were called or, you know, persons that had dressed up and were called Chetniks. Then there was the testimony that they had some special policy that was linked to the alleged ethnic cleansing, and I -- and cleansing of all non-Serbian population in Prijedor, and he has indicated that they were all Green Berets, and then I just wanted to find out does he know who those soldiers are and how they were linked to this policy and proceed. If the Prosecutor is bringing up to three or four witnesses --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: -- we do get a chance to explore it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll consider the relevance of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Vucicevic, the Chamber rules that this matter is not relevant. Move on to another question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, so if I understand you correctly -- if it's not relevant, it wouldn't be relevant for the Prosecutor to bring it up ever again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just move on and don't argue. We have made a ruling. If you wish to question it, you may do so in another arena. Move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, are you familiar with the term "Patriotic League"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] No. [Interpretation] I was not a member of any parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: If I can help you recall, Patriotic League was not a political party but a military organisation of Bosnian Muslims. Does it help you recollect?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does not jog my memory in any way. I don't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: When you were exchanged, do you know who -- at that time, who was the commanding officer of the Bosnian army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Sefer Halilovic jogs your memory?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have heard of that name.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: What was his function, if you do remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, but I only heard that he was either a unit commander or a commander of the BH army. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: He has written a book. Have you heard about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: So you didn't hear that he wrote a book; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not hear about it, and I don't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor asked you the question: "Witness G, what do you understand by the expression, 'cleanse the forest of Green Berets'?" And you answered: "It meant to me that they would look at all our people, Muslims or perhaps other ethnic background." Why did you identify Green Berets with all the Muslims and non-Serbs in the area in this answer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: When they incarcerated us in the camp, they only asked us about Green Berets, who they were, where they were, what their names were, and suchlike.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: You have testified about your past. Have you heard a term "Ustasha" ever?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what kind of uniforms and what kind of insignias did they have?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Listen, I cannot tell you with certainty. I know they looked pretty much like Chetniks because it's the same kind of organisation except that the former was on one side and the latter on the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: You just said that is what you heard through your membership of the party; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I saw the Ustasha on film too, when we did it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: So do you agree with me that both of these organisations were just pictured so bad by the ruling party that you belonged to; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, both were presented in a bad light, except that I participated in one of those when the film was made and I did not participate in the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of the war in Bosnia, in 1992, while Bosnian Muslims and Croats were at peace, have you ever heard the word "Ustasha" being uttered by any of the Muslim leadership at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not where I lived and worked, because we were together with Serbs, and one can check that any time who were my neighbours. And we indeed took care when there was war in Croatia, down in Kozarac because their houses were there and ours were right next to them, so that we were together at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... ceremony of tying of the flags in Sarajevo in 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only saw it on television. I know nothing else about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... and who were the persons you saw on TV doing it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: You just said that you saw it on the TV, you remember that you saw it, but you just don't know who were the persons there; right? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am from Kozarac and they are in Sarajevo. That is 300 kilometres away. And you mean I should know every single individual who lives in Bosnia there?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... but you just testified that you saw it on TV, so distance is not relevant. I'm asking just if you didn't remember --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Baly is on her feet.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to this line of questioning. It's not relevant and the witness' knowledge of it comes only from his viewing of television. He says he doesn't know who the persons were involved, and it should end there, in my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber agrees. Move on, Mr. Vucicevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: I have no more questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vucicevic. Re-examination, Ms. Baly?

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Witness G, you gave some evidence that three, four or five days prior to the massacre, a desk with sand bags and a machine-gun were placed. I have two questions. Firstly, who placed those items there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the guards, I suppose, the guards in the Keraterm camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Which way was the machine-gun facing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were facing the rooms where we slept.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: You were asked questions about whether inmates complained about beatings, and you said to the effect that if they did, they would end up on the garbage dump outside. What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant that if a soldier, one of the guards, asks you, "What's happened to you? Why is your head injured or your arm broken," or if you ever had any other visible bruises or you have blood on you, then he asks you, "What happened?" And if you say you were beaten, then he will ask you, "Who?" And if you know the name, and say it, as a rule, the next evening that person would be killed and dumped on garbage which was near the garage above Room 4.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Finally, Witness G, when detained at the Keraterm camp, were you a civilian person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a civilian throughout.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Those are my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Baly. Witness G, that completes your testimony. You may go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis, your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could briefly go into closed session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, closed session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'm providing the usher with copies of a document that contains identifying information with respect to this witness, and I would ask that he be shown a copy of that once it's been distributed to the parties and the Chamber. We are, in fact, in open session? Is that -- okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, I would ask you to look at the document that you've been provided and please verify that your name and date of birth are listed on that document.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd ask that this document be marked as the next exhibit in order, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit number 25.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, can you tell the Court, please, where you were born and where you were raised?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, Witness, you are a Muslim; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And in the year 1992, were you a civilian?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, I would like to draw your attention to June 1992. At that time, were you living in Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did there come a time when a group of soldiers arrived in your village and ordered you to dig graves?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please briefly describe what happened, to the Court?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I lived not far from the cemetery, a group of soldiers came and called my first cousin and me to the cemetery to dig four graves for people whom I did not know and who had been brought in plastic bags from the Trnopolje camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, in relation to where you were living in 1992, where was the Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was about 1.500 metres away from my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, Witness, during the same time period, that is, in June of 1992, did additional soldiers arrive and begin expelling the Muslim population from your village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, it was a daily occurrence, because it was a very big village. Every five or ten days, they would expel a street - well, I wouldn't call it a street, but a village road - and they would be coming to houses and plundering daily.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did this plundering also include rounding up of livestock and taking the livestock away?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, I'd like to draw your attention now to July of 1992. Have you ever heard of the Intervention Platoon Zoran Karlica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Prior to the 9th of July, I did not hear about that. It was the first day that I saw soldiers with patches saying "Zoran Karlica Intervention Platoon."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately when, what date or time frame that was in, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I saw soldiers with those patches, is that the question? When was it that I saw them?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was on the 9th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What did you see witnesses or -- excuse me. What did you see these soldiers with patches doing in your village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 9th of July, yes. The turn -- my street's turn came, and those soldiers grouped us together, separated men from women and took us down the village road to the Trnopolje camp. On the way, they ill-treated people, took out people from the group and killed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, you indicated that the men were separated from the women. When you were then marched down the street, which of those two groups of people were being marched down the street?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, naturally, men. Men were separated and were escorted by soldiers in the direction of the Trnopolje camp. And women went in different direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You indicated people were being mistreated. Can you briefly tell the Court what type of mistreatment occurred?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as we were on our way, we were beaten, made to sing songs, and within two hours at that time, 26 persons were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What kind of songs were you forced to sing, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, those were songs such as, "Who is Saying" -- "Who is Lying that Serbia is Small," "From Topola to Ravna Gora," and so on and so forth. And there was also some songs by Halid Muslimovic, "The Gypsy Girl," and the like.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You indicated, Witness, that 26 people were killed. Can you tell the Court what happened to those people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. During this transport to the camp, well, quite simply, those soldiers who were escorting us would take out some individuals, not that they knew them really, somebody had a cap on his head or a hat, or something specific. They just say to that man, "You come out," and kill him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How were these people killed, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, naturally, by gunshots.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, these people that were killed, do you know if they were soldiers or were they also civilians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were all civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Were all of the people -- all of the men from your village who were marched in the direction of Trnopolje camp, were they all civilians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were no soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, noting the time, before I move on to the next area, perhaps this might be an appropriate time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Witness H, we are going to take a break of half an hour. During the adjournment, you are not to discuss your evidence with anybody, and that includes members of the Prosecution team. We will adjourn until 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, immediately before the break, you were testifying about the men being marched toward the Trnopolje camp. Can you describe for us what happened after you arrived at the Trnopolje camp, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: The remaining survivors were lined up in front of the -- the hall of the Culture Club Bratstvo at Trnopolje, and they kept us there for two to three hours. It was raining. And we were mistreated there. We were beaten. Then they loaded us up in buses. In the back of the bus, there was standing-room alone. And we went down -- across Petrov Gaj, down a macadam road to Omarska. We stayed in -- on the bus for a while. They wouldn't let us out. Nobody boarded buses to mistreat us or anything, we just couldn't get out. Then we were transferred to Keraterm camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, do you recall the date and the approximate time that you arrived at the Keraterm camp, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the night of the 9th to 10 July 1992. We arrive at Keraterm camp at around 11.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, what happened to you and the other people on the bus upon your arrival at Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: A soldier boarded the bus and told us to get out, that five men from the rear section of the bus should go the -- come up front. And as we were passing by him, he would hit us wherever he -- and as we were dismounting, they just kept beating us. And when that was over, we came to another spot which was a small hut or like a reception area. This is where they took our documents from us and the valuables that we had on us. I personally was not beaten there. And just as I thought everything was over, we were met by four soldiers, and they told me to stop. One stepped on my feet and the two held me by arms and one of them said, "What are you looking at us?" And he cursed my mother, and he said, "We looked at you for 40 years." Then I got blows with a rifle butt and the rifle barrel in my chest and stomach. Then with the other people who had been beaten, I was lined up alongside the wall of Keraterm. When this torture was over with, then they ordered us to run to these halls. I did not know that this was Keraterm camp until that time, until I entered a room or hall 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, the individuals that were beating the detainees upon arrival, did you know any of those people that were doing the beating?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: That night, I did not. It was night-time, and I only recognised a person wearing a military camouflage uniform. He was -- his name was Zvonko. He was a physical education teacher in a primary school called 16 May, and then he had transferred to Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Were any of the other people that were doing the beating wearing any kind of uniform, and if so, what type of uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The person who beat us were wearing military camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, you indicated that you were placed in Room 2. Can you briefly describe for us the conditions in that room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were over 500 in this hall. The conditions, how shall I put it? The hygienic and other were very poor. The people who had been there before were -- looked exhausted and they were very -- they were -- they looked emaciated, and they were beaten up. There was a terrible smell in that hall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Was there a leader for that room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, if you can call it that. There was a person who was keeping the count of these men. He had lists.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What was that person's name, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fehim Krupic, called Feha.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, did there come a time when you were at Keraterm that you were taken for any kind of questioning or interrogation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was after my arrival at Keraterm, as I mentioned, between 9th and 10th. About ten days later, I went to the area above hall 1 and they may have also stretched over hall 2, and I went there for interrogation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did anything happen to you while you were on your way to the interrogation room? And if so, please tell us about that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was climbing the stairs, I don't know if you can say that I fared well. I only received one or two blows. When I entered the room, I found three men there. One was in civilian clothes, and the other two in military camouflage uniform. I recognised Mr. Simo Drljaca among them. For two or three minutes, they didn't ask me anything. They just stared at me. And then they asked me -- they asked me for my personal data, who I was, when I was born. I gave them my name and date of birth. They asked me my father's name. I told them. And they asked me where he was working. I told him that he worked at the Bratstvo Cultural Club at Trnopolje. At that point, one of these men whom I did not know kicked me Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25 from behind and said, "There is no more Bratstvo." Bratstvo means brotherhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Were you further mistreated at any time during the course of the interrogation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They took down information, who had what weapons. I did not know anything about it. And as far as beating is concerned, I was slapped several times, but they did not beat me on that occasion any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, I'd like to turn your attention now to the personnel in the camp. Were you aware of any kind of organisational structure with respect to the camp personnel? And if so, can you please describe that for us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that there was a structure. There was a commander of the camp. There were shift commanders. So I think that there was a structure there during my stay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall how many shifts there were at the Keraterm camp while you were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that there were three shifts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know who were in charge of those three shifts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The commander of one shift was Kole; of another one, Kajin; and a third one, Ustar or Fustar, I don't know exactly what his last name was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And do you know who was the overall commander of the camp during the time that you were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was Dusko Sikirica, and for a period of time, briefly, it was Kajin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let's start with the person you identified as Kole. Did you know him prior to the time that you arrived at the Keraterm camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Personally not. I knew him from town by sight.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately how many times you may have seen him before you arrived at the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before I was detained at the Keraterm camp? Is that the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was on a number of occasions in town. But I wasn't close to him. I did not communicate with him. It was all just in passing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall where you may have seen him in passing in town, what types of places you may have seen him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did see him in coffee bars, and on a number of occasions in Prijedor at the railway station and bus station. I was living in a village so I was there often and I saw him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you know his nickname prior to the time you arrived at Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: After your arrival at Keraterm, did someone inform you as to his nickname or name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I heard that from the other inmates.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, approximately how long were you in the Keraterm camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was there until the closure of the camp, which I think took place on the 5th or 6th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So it would be fair to say that you were there for slightly longer than three weeks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: During the course of those three weeks, approximately how many times did you see the person that was identified to you as Kole?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we were allowed to go outside, I could see him every time when his shift was on duty. So that meant, in effect, every other day or however their shifts changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, do you think you would recognise the person that you knew as Kole if you were to see him today?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honours. There was no foundation, sufficient foundation that was made, and before I make any further comments, I respectfully ask you to exclude the witness so I can point out the deficiencies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But you have already given us the basis of your objection, which is a lack of foundation, and I am not in a position, regrettably, to agree with that. I think the foundation has been laid. The Prosecutor asked the witness how many times he saw the person Kole, and he said he was in a position to see him virtually every other day. So I don't agree with the objection that you have made.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness has testified that he had seen him every other day or so in the camp, and there was no testimony on who and how sufficient was that identification in the camp. And prior to the camp, prior to the Keraterm, the witness being confined at Keraterm, the places and times are so general that it could have been somebody else that he had mistaken for Kole and then falsely identified him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We have heard your objection, and we rule that sufficient foundation has been laid. Go ahead, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, do you think that you would recognise the person whom was identified to you as Kole if you were to see him today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, I will ask you now to look around the courtroom, and if the person that you know as Kole is present, if you would please indicate that to the Court and tell us where in the courtroom he is sitting, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, objection. The witness has testified, "I think I would." He's not sure. So he would be guessing. I move that the identification be barred based on the witness' answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We overrule the objection. Go ahead, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, do you understand what I've asked you to do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, to point to the person whose name or nickname is Kole, and then you told me to look around the room. This is the gentleman, first to the right from -- to my right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Which row is the person that you've pointed out sitting in, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the second row.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And from your right to the left, if you could please count the seats and indicate the seat number of the person that you've identified, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: From right to left, in the first chair is a police officer, and the second seat is a man wearing civilian clothes, whose name or nickname is Kole.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd asked that the record reflect the witness has properly identified the accused Kolundzija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, I'd like to turn your attention now to the next shift commander that you identified, a person by the name of Kajin. Did you know that person from before the time that you were in the Keraterm camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did know him. That was a young man who did socialised with us. He would come to Trnopolje. And he had a girlfriend. He had -- who was a colleague, and to say her name, should I?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That's not necessary, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had a girlfriend, and he socialised with us. I even think he had some family in Petkovics.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, approximately -- for approximately how long prior to the time you were at Keraterm did you know this person Kajin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may have known him four or five years before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you briefly tell us what you mean when you say he socialised with you? What did that entail?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he liked to go to disco clubs and coffee bars, which I frequented too. He wasn't a close friend, but we would meet in the similar places.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you know his name or nickname prior to the time you arrived at Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, do you think you would recognise the person you knew as Kajin if you were to see him again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, I would ask you to again look around the courtroom and if the person that you know as Kajin is present, please indicate and describe for the Court where he is sitting.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The person is present. I will again start from right to left. It would be the fourth person from right to left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd ask that the witness has properly identified the accused Dosen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, let's turn now to the person that you've identified as the commander of the camp. Can you please tell us whether you knew that person prior to the time you arrived at the Keraterm camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally did not. I was not a close friend of him or I did not know him, but I saw him at my friend's at Kamicani. He also went into Kozarac. He had very good friends among Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you were in Keraterm that someone identified this person to you as the commander of the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I learned that from the inmates who were already there. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25 They knew. Both shift leaders ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, do you recall approximately how long it was after you had arrived at Keraterm that the other inmates described the camp commander to you or pointed him out to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps a few days later, two or three days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And during the time that you were at the Keraterm camp, did you see the camp commander frequently?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I could see him almost daily, provided the circumstances allowed, that is if we were not locked up in the halls, because we were, for the most part, in the halls.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, do you think you would recognise the person that you came to know as Sikirica if you were to see him today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, I would ask you to look around the courtroom, and if the person that was described to you as Sikirica, the commander of the camp, is present, please indicate to us where he is sitting.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will start again as before from right to left. It is the first -- the fifth person from right to left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd ask the record reflect that the witness has properly identified the accused Sikirica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, let's talk now about guards at the Keraterm camp. Did you know any of the guards at the Keraterm camp prior to the time you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I also knew them from town. The Banovic brothers, Predrag and Nenad. Their father was my teacher in the Rade Kondic elementary school in Kozarac. I also knew a number of other people by sight whom -- whose name I would not be able to tell, that is until I got there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, do you recall which shift the Banovic brothers were on during the time that you were at the Keraterm camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were in Kajin's shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, were there also other individuals who would -- who were not guards at the camp but who would nevertheless visit the camp and mistreat the detainees?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were persons who would enter the camp and mistreat people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall the names or nicknames of any of those individuals?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Duca, Ziga, Faca.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, do you know an individual by the name of Emsud Bahonjic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you see that person in the Keraterm camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you describe for the court the circumstances surrounding his death, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was taken out several times to be beaten. He was beaten up. And he was all broken up. They were calling him out under some nickname, and he died in hall 2 from the consequences of these beatings. He was broken up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, do you recall the nickname that they used when they called Emsud Bahonjic out of the room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They said the policeman from Kozarac; that's how they called him out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Was Emsud Bahonjic a policeman from Kozarac prior to the time that he was detained at Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, never. I was not involved in politics, but there was Territorial Defence before the war and they had their own police, and he was a member of that police force. That police force were wearing similar uniforms as the regular police at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, do you know what Emsud Bahonjic was beaten with?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why, yes, they beat him with batons, cables of all sorts, rods, rifle butts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Where did this beating occur at the Keraterm camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when they took him out at night, they took him somewhere. I think there was a room next to halls 3 and 4 where they beat those people. And once they also took him out in daytime, and they beat him from the entrance into hall 2 to the leftward, where there was a small room used for bread slicing, used to slice bread which we were given to eat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know who it was that beat Emsud Bahonjic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, it was Banovics, Ziga, and at night, I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, you've testified that he was beaten on several occasions. Do you know over a period of how long these beatings took place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. During my stay, what I know. He was the first one to die. And they took him out twice. But before that, I think they had left him alone for two or three days so that he would recover, and then they started it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know which shifts were on duty at the time Emsud Bahonjic was beaten?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that occasion that I know of, when I said that the Banovics were involved, it was Kajin's shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you describe any of the injuries that you saw on Emsud Bahonjic after he was beaten?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He had injuries on his head, his arm was broken, and so on and so forth. He had bruises around his ribs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know if Emsud Bahonjic was offered any type of medical treatment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not he.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, do you know a person by the name of Turkanovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you see that person in the Keraterm camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you describe for the court what happened to Turkanovic in Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: That man had very characteristic red hair, and once Bane called him out and said, "You, redhead, come out," and killed him with a baseball bat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you witness this happening? Did you see this happening?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was by daylight. He took him out, and since the door had bars, the door was open, so that we could have some air.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know who it was that did this to Turkanovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Banovic, called Cupo, Bane. I believe he is Predrag. There were two brothers, Predrag and Nenad.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you see what type of injuries Turkanovic received as a result of this beating, and if so, can you please describe them for the Court?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. His head. He had injuries to his head, and he died a short while later because he was beaten on the head. That is what I could see.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, do you recall where in the Keraterm camp Turkanovic died?
