utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why, yes, because it was also -- as I have said already, it was more or less on the same place where they had beaten up the previous gentleman, Emsud. Next to hall 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, do you know a person by the name of Fikret Avdic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was a waiter. He used to work for Cuiko coffee bar near the railway station in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you see Fikret Avdic in the Keraterm camp during the time that you were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us what happened to Fikret Avdic in Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once, and it was evening, he was called out. "Come on, Fikro, you. Come out, you, Fikro." They called out several times, and he responded. They told him he had a very nice name and last name. They took him out, and one could hear moans and sobs. And after a time, they brought him in front of hall 2 and told the inmates to carry him in. And he was at the top of hall 2. He was unconscious because he had been injured very badly, at least that is what I think. He was vomiting blood and water. He couldn't eat anything or speak. And in the morning, in the morning we took him out on a blanket in front of the hall and that is where he died. And they transferred him a bit higher up, moved him beyond Room 4 where there were dustbins, and that is where the bodies were taken out and away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, do you know which shift was on duty when Fikret Avdic was killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it was Mr. Kajin's shift once again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, do you know an individual by the name of Saban Elezovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you see him in the Keraterm camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you see him being mistreated at any time while you were in the Keraterm camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did. I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you describe that for us, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was taken out several times. He was one of the better of people in my locality, I should say, one of the wealthier men in Prijedor as a whole. He was taken out several times and beaten, questioned about money and cars, and his arms were broken. I do not know exactly, but I think that on one occasion, Mr. Kajin, how, I don't know, took him to the hospital, and he returned with a plaster cast.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know which shift was on duty when Saban Elezovic was Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25 beaten?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was taken out on various occasions. I'm not sure whether it was Fustar's shift and Kole's shift and Kajin's too, but when he was killed, it was Banovics who did it. They beat him up and he succumbed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, do you know a person by the name of Mesic and did you see that person in Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did. I wouldn't know his first name, but his last name was Mesic. He was in Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you see Mesic being mistreated during the time you were in Keraterm, and if so, can you please describe that for us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, we were outside once. He was a middle-aged man. And I don't know why it was that they forced us to get back inside quickly. And he just hesitated for a moment and was struck with a baseball bat on the head so that his skull was fractured. He somehow made it to the hall and there he died.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know who was responsible for this beating? Who beat Mr. Mesic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there in the camp, his beating -- there was Faca also too, but Banovics. There was Ziga.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, do you recall an incident when Ziga fired a pistol into your room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us about that incident, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he came on that occasion and said verbatim, "Turks, balijas, Ziga's come to visit you. You're balijas number two." And we all tried to escape to the bottom of the room because we knew what would happen, and we were all one on top of the other. He took out his pistol and fired at the ceiling, and it ricochetted and hit this man in the leg. Another inmate said that the man -- "The man is wounded," so -- and he said then, "So what? His throat should be then slit so that he does not suffer."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall who it was that said his throat has to be slit so he wouldn't suffer? Who said that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Zigic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall the name of the person who was hit by the ricochetted bullet?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not quite, but I think he came from somewhere in Jakupovici or something. I didn't really know him because there were so many of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, prior to the incident that's been described as the Room 3 massacre, did you hear gunshots on any other occasions while you were at Keraterm after Zigic fired the pistol?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were gunshots.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you see any of the detainees being shot prior to the Room 3 massacre while you were in the Keraterm camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, are you asking me was somebody killed in Room 3 or before that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Before that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Was somebody killed in Room 3 or outside Room 3? That is what I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, do you recall a detainee being shot while he was on the way to the toilet?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please describe that incident for the Court?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were in Room -- in hall 2 with a big door, and I was next to the door, and I could look through the bars because there were no windows. And the gentleman, Mr. Sikirica, was there. And the man was going to the toilet, and from about 20 or 30 metres, he killed him with a pistol. He fired at him two or three times. The man fell. And then he came up and put his foot on his head, and then he passed by hall number 2. And after a while, he took a car and left the camp in -- and I don't know in which direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, you testified that he killed him with a pistol. Who fired the pistol?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said it already, that it was Mr. Sikirica who fired the pistol.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, do you know who the victim of that shooting was? Did you know the person who was shot?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He had blue jeans, a T-shirt and sneakers. I didn't know him. I think -- I think he came from so-called Brdo area, that is Hambarine, Ristanovici, that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, can you tell us about the conditions in Room 3 prior to the arrival of the individuals from Brdo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that hall 3 was next to the lavatories or the toilets. In those toilets, there was urine some ten centimetres deep, and it leaked into hall 3 and the stench was horrible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall a time when a large number of men arrived from the -- from the Brdo area? And if so, can you tell us approximately when that was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think it was sometime on the 17th, 18th, maybe the 19th, August, when people got there. They were lying down on the pista, and they were mistreated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, for clarification, which month was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court what shift was on duty when these people from Brdo arrived?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: When they arrived? I think it was Fustar's shift when they arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you describe for the Court what happened to these people when they first arrived, in their first few days in Keraterm camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were locked, incarcerated in hall 3. Those -- for three or four days, those men were not given any food, they were not let out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you describe for us the events that occurred on the day of the massacre in Room 3, starting from, say, 6.00 p.m. in the evening that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as of 6.00 that afternoon, I couldn't really tell you because I had no watch, but shifts were changing and Mr. Kole with his guards came on and then it started. Some moves -- we were inside in hall number 2, and there were those weapons which were there. And after a while, one could hear voices, noises. One could hear some vehicles coming into the camp, shouts, singing. And those men who were locked there, they were already in such a bad shape that one could hear the noise they were making. And around 11.00 or 12.00 at night, gunfire started. One could hear moans and sobbing. I am not sure but I think that I heard Kole's voice, saying to those men, "Who is going to account for this?" And told them not to open fire on other halls because those people were not responsible. But the gunfire went on until 4.00 or 5.00 in the morning, when it died out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, can you tell us what kind of gunfire you heard that evening?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why, yes, from firearms, one could hear both individual shots and rounds of fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, do you recall any of the smells or odours that were in the camp on that evening?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. One could smell something like tear gas. Tear gas was thrown at them because it has a specific smell, and of course it itches your eyes and the mucous and the nerves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The following morning, Witness, were you able to see anything out of your room with respect to Room 3?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They would not let us go out to the lavatory, and then eventually they let us go there one by one. And in front of hall 3, I saw several bodies. But I was really running because that is how I had to go to the lavatory and back. I could not see the interior of hall 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did there come a time when anything was done with respect to removing the bodies? And if so, can you please tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Sometime around 8.00, the shift commander of that morning shift, Kajin's shift, came in front of hall 2 and asked, "Who will come out?" His truck had arrived. "Who will come to load those men on the truck?" Because men had been massacred, killed by those firearms, and that he was guaranteeing that the men who came out on that occasion would also return to hall 2, that they would not be killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you describe for us the loading of the truck that morning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two men from my room went to do it. I knew them. Hazim Sivac and Bahrija Sivac. They threw those men onto that truck, onto a trailer - what do you call it? - and there was blood running down the sides of the truck.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What happened to the truck?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: As they were -- after they were loaded, the truck left in an unknown direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you ever see that truck again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It came back in the afternoon, and then it was washed in the camp compound. One could observe on the wheels of that truck something like red slag.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Had you ever seen red slag like that before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why, yes. There, in the vicinity of Prijedor, we had those open cast mines, Omarska, Tomasica, and this reddish earth was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis, I don't think there's been any evidence about this. Have any of these bodies been recovered or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, there will be evidence presented on that matter later in the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Where were they recovered from?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: There were -- Your Honour, there were, to the best of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25 my recollection, three or four sites from which bodies were recovered. We have reports from expert witnesses on this matter, which will be hopefully introduced later in the trial or pursuant to 94 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, let me just ask you a question about Hazim Sivac and Bahrija Sivac, the two men from your room who loaded the truck. Did you ever see them again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those men did return to Room number 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did they tell you anything about the number of bodies that they loaded onto the truck?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They said precisely that those men had been massacred and that they thought there were between 160 to 200 men, because amongst those men there were also -- there were also some wounded who were taken in that same truck who had survived the massacre, and I believe they had been wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, were there -- to your knowledge, were there other individuals who survived the Room 3 massacre without being wounded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that some did survive. There could have been four or five of them who were then put in different rooms and who happened to be under those bodies and who had been only lightly wounded and, therefore, did not report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, are you aware of another incident where a guard named Faca shot a prisoner in the Keraterm camp, and if so, can you please describe that for us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the room where we were, at the very entrance to the room there was a barrel where we relieved ourselves, and one night, a man who was on that barrel was killed. This man called Faca came in, and he said, "Are you a policeman from Kozarac," or, "Are you from Brdo," or something like that, and from a distance of two or three metres, he shot at the man. And the man just moaned and said, "Oh, you killed me," and he dropped dead there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, in the final days before the Keraterm camp was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis, is he able to say on whose shift that incident occurred?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, do you know which shift was on duty when this man was shot?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: The night when he was killed, I think it was Kajin's shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Witness, in the final days before the Keraterm camp was closed, were there other incidents when you personally were mistreated at the Keraterm camp, and, if so, can you please describe those for the Court?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On one occasion - I think it was on the 19th or the 30th of July, just before the closure of the Keraterm camp, four or five days - I went to get -- fill some water, and Cupo Banovic was there. He asked me, "Where are you going?" And I said, "To fill some water." And he said, "Do you know that we -- you have to pay for water?" And I said I didn't have any money. Then he took off his shoes and started beating me with them over my head. He broke my nose. And meanwhile, at the gate, Kajin, who was the shift commander, arrived on a small motorcycle. At that point, he pulled a knife and wanted to stab me in my left side. I instinctively raised my arms, and he cut me across my left arm 10 to 13 centimetres. I could see my bone. And he said, "Go back to the room." Then later on he called me out, but I did not respond. Also, on another occasion, he beat me up. He knocked out the front tooth on my upper jaw. I had -- my lips and my jaw were injured.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, do you have any scar from the time when you were stabbed in the Keraterm camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I still have the scars, and the scars on my lips are still there and my tooth is still broken.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, with the permission of the court, I would ask the witness to pull up his shirt sleeve and show the court the scar which remains from the stabbing incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Vucicevic is on his feet. Yes, Mr. Vucicevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: We certainly do not dispute that it occurred, and I don't think it would be any need for theatrics, as Your Honour observed earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't think we need this evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, you testified earlier that the camp closed on approximately the 5th or 6th of August, 1992. Can you tell us what happened on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the morning, Messrs. Kajin and Sikirica were both there, and they arrived to the area between halls 1 and 2 and they said, "Those men whose names we will read out will be transferred to the Omarska camp. The remainder of the men will be taken in buses to Trnopolje camp." Then the list was read of the men, who would then step out, and as they were boarding buses, they were being beaten. These buses went, and from what I heard from other people, they were taken to Omarska and nothing is known of these men. It was two bus loads of men. And the other inmates of Keraterm camp, 12 or 13 bus loads were transferred to Trnopolje camp. I was in these buses that were going from Orlovci, Garici to Trnopolje. Two or three buses went along the main Prijedor-Banja Luka highway, and they took that route. But later on, these buses also arrived at Trnopolje camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, do you recall who read out the names on the lists of which person would go to which camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it was Mr. Sikirica who read those names.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And it's correct that you were on one of the buses that went to the Trnopolje camp; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you briefly tell us what the conditions were like in Trnopolje when you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unlike Keraterm camp, the conditions were better. When we arrived there, they locked us up. I personally left the Keraterm camp weighing 48, 49 kilograms. I could not walk on my own power. They unloaded us within the perimeter which was fenced. They did not allow us to contact -- to make contact with other people in Trnopolje camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, you indicated when you left Keraterm you weighed 48 or 49 kilograms. How much did you weigh when you first arrived at Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I weighed 67 kilograms, and that was my normal weight.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, while were you in Trnopolje, did you see any prisoners being badly treated or killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were murders committed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, Prosecution has no further questions for this witness at this time, but I would like to simply make a clarification with respect to the question that Judge May asked earlier. With the benefit of the technology that we have available in the courtroom, I have received indications from another member of our team that although we will have evidence with respect to three or four sites where bodies were recovered, we have been unable to link any of those bodies to the bodies that were taken away from Room 3 in the aftermath of the massacre. So I simply wanted to clarify that, that we have not been able to link any of the bodies that we have recovered to -- specifically to the Room 3 massacre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours? If I may, objection. Since the Prosecutor has presented the evidence on the colour of the trucks after the bodies were taken away, that testimony presents simple conjecture, and at this time I move that all that testimony about the colours and possible locations be stricken from the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That is a matter which we will assess. I mean, that's our function. We will assess that evidence and make what we will of it. Mr. Greaves?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Yes. May we go into private session, please, for a moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Witness H, when you made your statement to the Office of the Prosecutor in January, 1995, you were interviewed by somebody called Thomas Ackheim, and there were two interpreters present; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: There was somebody else present at that interview, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right now, I cannot recall. I know that there were two interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Somebody called Mohamed Susic? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Who was Mohamed Susic, Witness H?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am unable to tell you that. I don't know the man.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Was he someone from the Bosnian army supervising what you were telling the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Could we turn now, please, to some of the events in June 1992, please. The people who were buried in the graveyard near to your home, you did not know either their names or the ethnicity of those people, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Four bodies, as I stated, arrived in plastic bags, and I also stated that I was forced, because my house was there, to also bury people from Trnopolje. I knew some of those people's names, but those in June, those names I did not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Isn't this right, that when the bodies were brought to the graveyard, they were in black plastic bags and, therefore, you were not on any occasion able to see who was inside?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We could not see.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Do you recall making a statement to the Bosnian authorities on the 3rd of November, 1994?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. To the Bosnian authorities?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Yes. The 3rd of November, 1994.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: May we just go into private session again, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We are now in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Why didn't you mention the names of the people you were able to identify to the Bosnian authorities then, Witness H?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I did mention the names. Hrnic Himzo, Safet Kararic. That those names are there because I knew these men. I was able to recognise them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Will you help us about this, please? The intervention platoon which had the name Karlica, was that named for a former commander of that unit who had been killed during fighting in Prijedor in either April or May 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Did you know the name of the commander at the time when they came to your location?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Or his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the soldiers who came there were of Serbian faith. They were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: There was a group of people who were killed at that time by five or six soldiers. Were they part of the intervention platoon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: In total, how many people were detained with you at the same time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that in reference to the Keraterm camp, how many people were detained in Room 2?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: When you were first detained in Trnopolje and taken away, how many people were detained with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was during the transportation, when they transported us. My street was about one kilometre long, and there was some refugees there. We were up to 60, 70. And when we joined the other road, they -- other people from Durici, Elezi and other streets joined us. And when we arrived at Trnopolje, the whole transport numbered up to 200 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And were those all men, Witness H?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were some who were elderly, and there were some who were underage.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Have you been discussing what evidence has been given before this Tribunal with anybody else, who either has or is about to give evidence, Witness H?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: You anticipated, I suggest, my next question, which was to be about the age of the people who were detained with you. How did you know that that was going to be part of the questioning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not know that, but this is how I stated it. I wanted to point out that there were people of different ages, that there were people who were above 60 and 70, and then there were minors among them, too, because they collected everyone, all males, regardless of age, everybody who was over 15 or 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to move to another topic in a moment, and I think it's now 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness H, we are going to take the adjournment until 1.30. During the adjournment, you are not to discuss your evidence with anybody, including members of the Prosecution team. We are adjourned.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may address the court before you retire for lunch, but just after the witness walks out because there is a logistical matter that is very timely sensitive, nothing to do with what transpired today, but I would just like to bring it to your attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness be escorted. After the witness has been escorted out, we will hear from Mr. Vucicevic. Mr. Greaves?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour said that we would be adjourned until 1.30. Did you actually mean that? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I wouldn't rob you of that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: And if we could be just in a closed session because I don't know whether the identities of the people I am going to mention have been so far disclosed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.05 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Greaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Witness H, having been detained along with other people, you were taken first to Omarska in buses. It's right, isn't it, that you were kept there for two hours before going on to Keraterm? Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: They kept us. For how long I don't know, maybe two or four hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And were you turned away from Omarska because Omarska was found, at the end of that period, to be full and, therefore, there was no capacity to take your group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no way of knowing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: In the statement which you made to the Bosnian authorities in November 1994, you told them this: "They took us in buses to Omarska camp, but we were not admitted there because the camp was already full." So you plainly new in 1994 the reason you couldn't go to Omarska, didn't you, Witness H?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not know the reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: If you didn't know the reason, why did you claim to the Bosnian authorities that you did know the reason?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not claim it before the Bosnian authorities. I never made such a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Let's turn now to your interrogation, Witness H. You've told us that three people were present during that, one of whom was Simo Drljaca. How was Simo Drljaca dressed when he interrogated you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: The gentleman was in a uniform. He had a uniform, a blue, olive-green/blue one, the camouflage uniform, the police uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: So specifically the police uniform, not a military uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Police, military, and civilian during my interrogation, and I said that quite clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: There was a second man in military clothing. Did you know him at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: The third man was dressed in civilian clothing. Did you know that person at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. No. No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Which is it, Witness H, you did or you didn't know him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew Mr. Simo Drljaca. The man in the military uniform and the civilian I did not know, and I did not say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Which of the three men asked you the questions, Simo Drljaca, the other man in military clothing, or the civilian?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were cross-examining me, all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: So all three men asked you questions. Can you explain then, please, why it is you told the Office of the Prosecutor: "The man in camouflage uniform looked at me and Drljaca started to question me. He asked me questions about my personal background and my previous military experience"? Why did you say it was Simo Drljaca who questioned you and not that you were cross-examined by the three?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said clearly, when I entered that room, for a while they did not interrogate me. They just stared at me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Apart from the men who interrogated you, did you know the name of any other person who was involved in interrogating witnesses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that there were three men, and of them all, I knew Simo Drljaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Sorry. I asked that question badly. Used the word "witnesses" when I shouldn't have done so. I'll ask it again. Apart from the men who interrogated you, Witness H, did you know the name of any other person who was involved in interrogating other detainees?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I had no access to other rooms where prisoners were interrogated.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: So the only people -- in fact, the only person of whom you knew the name who was involved in any way in interrogating any detainee is the man Simo Drljaca; is that the position?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, naturally. Until that interrogation, we were escorted by guards who were there in those rooms.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Why did you tell the Bosnian authorities in November, 1994, then, this? "The interrogators were from Prijedor. They were accompanied by Simo Drljaca, chief of the SJP Public Security Station in Prijedor, and Slavko Torbica, a.k.a. Cune from Sanicani, a member of the special police unit from Banja Luka"? Why were you able then to give a name when you say now that you didn't know the names of anybody else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say that. All I said was that that gentleman who worked at Sanicani used to come to the Keraterm camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Which of the three men in the room beat you? Was it Drljaca, the civilian or the man in the -- the other man in military clothing, Witness H?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was beaten -- well, not beaten but, as I said, kicked me so that I fell off that chair and slapped me a couple of times, and that was done by the man in the military uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Apart from giving statements to the Bosnian authorities and a written statement to the Office of the Prosecutor, you were interviewed, were you not, before making the statement to the Office of the Prosecutor by a representative of the OTP? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Did you not say at some stage to some representative of the Office of the Prosecutor that you were only interrogated by two men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I said clearly that there were three men. One stared at me at the beginning and asked me nothing and then they cross-examined me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Can you describe to us the offices where these interrogations took place, Witness H?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot describe those offices. I can describe the office that I was in.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Tell us what it looked like, then, Witness H.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you enter that room, to the left and there were two or three desks where those three men were, and the chair that I sat on was a metre and something from the door and also about one metre from the wall, facing those men.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Was this the only occasion when you saw Simo Drljaca in Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, people were interrogated every day. A minibus would come to bring them in. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: You've just told us that this was the only occasion on which you saw Simo Drljaca in Keraterm. Why did you tell the Office of the Prosecutor in January 1995 that you saw him about ten times in the camp, Witness H?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say now that I only saw him once. I only said that I personally saw him in that room when he interrogated me. Mr. Drljaca would come in that van, in that van there, and that is how I could see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Did you become aware, or did you know of your own knowledge, that it was Simo Drljaca who made decisions about where detainees would be sent?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I couldn't know that he was the one who decided about those things, and who made those decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Did you know of somebody at the camp on the staff called Zivko Knezevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew people's nicknames and their faces, and I've already said those whom I knew personally, so to tell you who Zivko Knezevic was, I can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: We've heard from other witnesses that a new commander arrived at the camp sometime around the 27th of July, 1992. Were you aware of that, Witness H?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: The new commander arrived on the 27th of July? Well, I said that I arrived there on the 9th of July, and that one, if you mean Mr. Sikirica, he was already there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: No, Witness H. We do not mean Sikirica. It's right, isn't it, that a new commander arrived around the 27th of July, shortly before you left Keraterm? Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which new commander you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: You told Their Honours this morning, in relation to Dusko Sikirica, that you were told within two or three days of arriving who he was.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that clearly, that I had heard it from people who had been detained there before me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honours, just give me a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: How could that be, Witness H, if according to you in your statement to the Office of the Prosecutor, he didn't even arrive at the camp for seven to ten days after your arrival?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say that. When I arrived in the camp, I said that from some people who were already there, heard that the camp commander was Mr. Sikirica.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Witness H, let me just give you and remind you a little bit of the detail of what you said to the Office of the Prosecutor and put into your written statement that you made in January 1995. You spoke of the commander of the camp when you first arrived, someone you knew because you knew his grandparents, and you said this: "Seven to ten days after my arrival, he was replaced by Sikirica. I did not know him from before, but I was told by other prisoners that he worked at the railroad company in Prijedor." That's what you were saying in January 1995. Why did you say that if it isn't true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said it quite clearly, that upon my arrival, not seven or ten days, that there was Mr. Damir Dosen Kajin and that he was replaced - that is what my statement says - because he had been taking some people to the hospital and those people were coming back alive and that his place was taken by Mr. Sikirica.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Do you understand, Witness H, that in that statement, you were telling the Prosecutor that Sikirica did not even arrive to take over as commander until seven to ten days after your arrival? And the point is this: How could you then be told, within two or three days of your arrival, that Sikirica was the commander? Please explain the difference between those two things. Their Honours might like to know.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said clearly that when I arrived at the camp in Keraterm there was Mr. Dosen, that he was replaced by Mr. Sikirica. And if it says up to ten days, well, it could be a slip. What I heard from the inmates, in two or three days, that Mr. Sikirica was the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And the information, so that we can just get this clear, that you were given by other prisoners also included the information that the man you were told was Sikirica had worked at the railway company; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, I did not know the gentleman personally. I wasn't his friend or something. But I knew him from Kozarac because he used to go there. And personally that I stated that he worked for a railway company, no. I said I think he worked there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Why didn't you tell the Office of the Prosecutor in January 1995 that you'd seen this man before the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps nobody asked me that. Because I did not know the man personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: You were telling the Office of the Prosecutor you didn't know this man from before the war, weren't you, and this is something you've simply made up in the meantime?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I did not say that I had never seen him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: The person that you knew as Dusko Sikirica in Keraterm, what did he look like? Just describe him, age, height, build, those sort of things.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the gentleman is about my height. He was -- well, perhaps he had some more weight than now, and he had a moustache.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: How old was he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot say for sure, but he must -- I'd say that he was born sometime around 1964. 1963, 1964. I have no way of knowing it. Perhaps slightly older.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And just tell us something about his -- your height so that we can measure your estimate of his height. How tall are you, Witness H?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: A hundred and sixty-seven, eight centimetres.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: The man that you've described, was he always armed or sometimes armed or never armed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: That person always carried a pistol.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Just an ordinary semi-automatic pistol of the kind that most military men carry?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was a bigger pistol than the ordinary ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: You've described the killing of somebody by the man you have called Sikirica and that he drove off after the event, went off after the event. What sort of vehicle did he leave in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I said that the vehicle was --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We apologise. We could not hear the end of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness H, would you repeat the answer. The interpreter didn't get all of it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the gentleman left in a -- in a white Golf.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Let's just now examine what you claim was a killing by this man Sikirica. At what time of day did this take place, Witness H?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was sometime in the afternoon, sometime around 2.00 or 3.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: So in full daylight. No question of it being at night-time; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. If it's daylight, then why do you need lights?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Before the inmate was shot, what was the man you've described as Dusko Sikirica doing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was in the camp. He was standing from halls 1 and 2 facing toward the reception hut that was there. He was in the compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Perhaps you'd just like to have a look at some photographs in Exhibit 2, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Would you just show the witness the book of photographs?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Witness H, without saying anything, just look through that book of photographs, would you please, and look at each photograph? And then I'm going to ask you some questions about it. If you'd like to retain them, please, Witness H, I'm going to ask you some questions about them. Are those photographs of Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Is there a photograph in that bundle of photographs where you can identify where it was that the man you've called Dusko Sikirica was standing when he shot the inmate? And if so, would you be so kind as to have it put on the ELMO and point it out to us? Have you seen anything on there, Witness H, that you can identify for us?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I think he will also need the pointer, if you could please give him that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Can you point to where you think it happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates]. This is the reception hut where we came, and behind is the Keraterm compound. You can see clearly here the lampposts. One of them, you can see one of them. And they were positioned -- they were spaced out. This one was at the beginning. Now, this has been redone. It looks differently now. And there was hall 2, and next to it hall 2 -- hall 1, hall 2. The gentleman was in front of those entrances into halls 1 and 2 -- well, about ten metres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And walking in which direction?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was facing the reception office. He was walking facing the reception office.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And by "the reception office," you mean that building, rectangular building, that we can see in the forefront of the photograph? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This one, this hut here, this hut here, with two bicycles.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: So he was walking away from the big building that we can see in the background towards the reception hut; is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Faced this reception hut here, here, right here. He was standing on the pista.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: We're talking now about the inmate. Are you talking about the inmate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You asked me about the gentleman, where he stood, I mean Mr. Sikirica. And the inmate, the inmate, hall number 1, number 2, and then WC, so one can see it well here. This reception office and the lawn and the grassy area, and that is where he was lying. From this lamppost to the second lamppost, it is about 20, 30 metres, and that is where it happened between them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: So at the time when it happened, the inmate was walking away from the man who shot him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. That inmate was ill-treated that whole day right here in this spot which you can see. No, he wasn't walking.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Well, how was he making his way from the room to the toilet, if he wasn't walking?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stated clearly that the prisoner was here on the grassy area, not in the room. He wasn't going from the room. He had spent all day there, and that's where he was mistreated and abused, between the toilet and this area here, the grassy area.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Please would you explain to us, then, if that is the position concerning the man who was shot by the man you've claimed was Dusko Sikirica, that you told the Office of the Prosecutor this: "He went from Room number 3 towards the toilet." Please can you explain the discrepancy between what you have just told us and what you told the Office of the Prosecutor, Witness H?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you see, this area here, this is a big area of earth, and this man was near that room on that grassy area across from Room 3. And it was obvious that if he was going to the toilet that he would pass by the entrance to Room 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: When the man was shot, was he facing or facing away from the man you've called Dusko Sikirica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was facing him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: When he was shot, did he die immediately?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There were two or three shots. Not after the first shot, he didn't even fall. After second or third, he did fall.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: If this incident took place at 2.00 or 3.00 in the afternoon in high summer in Bosnia, why did you tell the Bosnian authorities that it had taken place one night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Let me remind you of what you told the Bosnian authorities, Witness H. "I saw him with my own eyes one night and that was the night before the mass killing of inmates in hall number 3. He was standing near the lavatory between halls 2 and 3, leaning against a post and shooting at an inmate who was going to the lavatory." That's what you told the Bosnian gentleman, Mr. Ibric. Please can you explain why you told Mr. Ibric that if it actually took place in the middle of the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that. If I did say that to the investigative magistrates, I was only referring to the fact that it had happened two or three nights before the massacre, not that it happened during the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Are you sure this incident happened, Witness H?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: You see, I suggest to you that it's something you've simply made up. Isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, that is your opinion. That would mean that I'm lying.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And you simply can't remember the detail well enough to get your story straight more than once running, can you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember the killing sufficiently well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And if it did happen, I suggest to you it certainly wasn't the man you've identified in court as Dusko Sikirica, was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that he was, as I asserted.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Let's move on to another topic, Witness H. Can you help us with this, the incident involving Emsud Bahonjic? First of all, can you give us a date for that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I clearly said that the man was taken out on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And is this right: He was beaten because he was in the TO at Kozarac and was in the reserve police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't clear on that, but when they called him out, they called him "the policeman from Kozarac."

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Fikret Avdic. Can you identify a date when that incident took place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: That may also have -- could have been in mid-July, between the 18th or 20th. Around that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And is this right, that one of the guards, a man called Kondic, wanted to take his clothes from him and that's why he was assaulted?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: The man Elezovic who was assaulted, can you give us a date for that incident? Would it be around the end of July, the very end of July 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: This man was also taken out on several occasions, and the murder took place in July.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: You told the Office of the Prosecutor that it was the end of July. Does that refresh your memory as to the date, Witness H?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After all this time and all of this, I cannot give the exact date. I know the exact date of when I was beaten, when my close family was killed. That I remember very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And the man whose name -- first name you don't know but second name, Mesic, a professor, did you put a date on that, when that incident happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: All this took place in July.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And was the reason that he reacted too slowly to a call to go back to the room that he was shot? Or assaulted, rather.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible. It depended on the shift when we would go out. So then they would let us out to breathe some air for a few minutes, and we would run back in. It is possible, because he was a bit heavier and he lagged behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: The man called Cupo Banovic, it's right, isn't it, that he tried to extort money from you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When I went to fill the water and go to the toilet.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: The two Banovic brothers were there. It's right, isn't it, that that's what they specialised in, trying to extort money from prisoners? Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were two Banovic brothers. That was a regular thing, to take money and gold and watches. Not only by the two of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I want to ask you now, Witness H, about the time when the camp was closed on the 5th or 6th of August, 1992. There was a group of prisoners who went to Omarska on buses. Was there anything that happened physically to them, apart from a beating, before they went to Omarska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were prisoners from these halls. Of course, these were -- among them there were men who were beaten. They were called out. There was a list that was read out and these people came -- were coming out.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honours, just give me a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Yes. But apart from people being beaten who were in this group that went to Omarska at the time of the closure of the camp, was there anything else physical that was done to them in any way at all before they went off to Omarska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before that, there was a review in the camp, and it was said that those who were exhausted and sick would be transferred, and personal data was taken about their education and work background.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: You've told Their Honours that Sikirica and Kajin were present on the occasion when those people left for Omarska, and you've described how names were read out from a list. The very first time you've ever mentioned that was this morning here in court about that, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: So far, nobody had asked me who was present, and of course, I said who was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: You didn't tell the Bosnian authorities that Sikirica and Kajin were involved in that, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not tell the Bosnian authorities about my knowledge, but I did talk to the persons who came from the Tribunal, and you mentioned their names. I don't recall them any more. And had I given any statement to the Bosnian authorities, it -- it is possible that I did not know that some of them may have been a member of the Bosnian authorities, but if -- I did not give any statement to the Bosnian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: So are you saying that you gave the information about Sikirica and Kajin to those people whose names we talked about, in 1995? Is that when you say that you mentioned it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not what I said. You asked me clearly whether I had -- I had stated this morning that these persons were present, and it is true, they were present. And whether I had told this to those people or not, this -- these -- these men were present, Mr. Dosen and Mr. Sikirica, while the list was being read out.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Did Mr. Mundis, who has been talking to you, I think, recently, did he ask you who was present when the buses went off to Omarska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is possible that he asked me who was present.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Did you tell him? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I stated, I said, as I told you this morning, that Mr. Sikirica and Mr. Kajin were both present, and whether I had said it to the person who was questioning me, that I cannot say. They were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: You're quite sure you haven't been talking to other witnesses about what's been going on in this Tribunal concerning this case, Witness H?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: The reason that it's not mentioned in either your statement to the Bosnian authorities or to the Office of the Prosecutor, I suggest, is because you didn't witness such a thing, Witness H, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I have clear proof that I was in Keraterm and Trnopolje camps from the ICRC, from Geneva.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Witness H, I hadn't suggested that you weren't. Why are you so anxious to suggest to us that you can prove it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because you, sir, are saying that I did not see this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Just finally, Witness H, the two places where you were detained, Keraterm and Trnopolje, they had a substantial number of people detained there, did they not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were a lot of people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: How many were detained, according to you, in Keraterm at any one time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that - this was when we were leaving Keraterm to go to Trnopolje - at that time, there were between 1.000 and 1200 people, and because people were killed, I think that at some point there must have been 1500 or 1600 people. And in Trnopolje camp, there were a lot more people.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Several thousand?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And throughout the time when you were detained in those two places, the people -- you yourself and those other people were entirely in the power of the Serb authorities, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Around these camps, the checkpoints were set up, manned by Serb soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And it's right, isn't it, that at both the two camps, Keraterm and Trnopolje, there was nothing to prevent the Serb authorities from killing all of you at any time? Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not competent to say something like this, but given the number of killings, that means that people could do whatever they wanted to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: If Your Honour would just give me a moment, please? Your Honour, save to ask that his statement to the Bosnian authorities and to the OTP should be exhibited, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. They will be exhibited. Mr. Petrovic, I neglected to mention that today we will stop at 4.00 p.m. as the Chamber is involved in another matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness H, I would like to first clarify a point which you were trying to clear up with Mr. Greaves. Mr. Greaves had asked you whether you had given a statement to the Bosnian authorities. You told him that you had not. Two minutes later, he again asked you whether you had given a statement to the Bosnian authorities, and you said that you did. Which of these is true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say yes. I said that if somebody was present or was there who -- of the Bosnian authorities, who was with the investigators of the Tribunal, that is possible, but not that I gave it directly to the Bosnian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How many people were present when you gave the statement to the investigators of the ICTY?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was the investigator, there was an interpreter, and I think another interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And then they compiled the statement in front of you and then you signed that statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. When I gave a statement to the authorities from the Tribunal, I did sign it, but not the one to the Bosnian authorities.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can we have the counsel --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies. The microphone was not on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you the question again. When you gave the statement to the Tribunal investigators, you signed it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: On that occasion, you only signed that statement? That is the only existing statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In other words, you only signed one statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I stated it clearly, if those were the people --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Let's take it very easy. You signed one statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, to the gentleman from the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you read that statement before signing it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I gave the statement, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Was this statement in the Bosnian language?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I please ask the usher's assistance to show the witness a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Will you please review this document. And you'll see the statement, and if I can just ask you to look down and see what is also stated at the bottom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Will you please read it out loud.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you want me --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, do not read anything right now. Is that your name, your personal data?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Will you now please look at the bottom left corner.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Will you please turn to the second page. At the bottom right corner, do you also see your signature?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Will you please check the remainder of the pages. Do you see your signature on them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: But this was -- this is nothing to do with the war crimes and this was not to the Bosnian --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Will you please just return the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: There was overlapping. Please observe the pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, my apologies, Your Honour. I would like the usher to please return the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So we have determined that each of these pages bears your signature.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: On the last page that you signed, it states: "The citizen has read the statement and has no objection to it whatsoever. He's prepared to give this entire testimony in a court of law or before some international organisation and to make a new statement in the event that he remembers any additional details."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: That statement was given when I first arrived in Travnik when I was expelled and when they were taking down my personal data and when they asked me what I had gone through, and I did not give any statement regarding the Tribunal and things like that, but those people were not from the state security or something that you have been suggesting.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What did these people ask you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: About my life story, where I was in camps, what happened there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And what did the people from the Tribunal ask you, something else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is true that they asked me these things, but they asked me whether I would testify about what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Why did you this morning tell us twice that you had not given any statement to the Bosnian authorities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how many times I need to repeat it. When I was questioned and when the gentleman from The Hague Tribunal came, it is possible that there were some members of the local authorities there and that they made that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So when did you sign this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be honest, I certainly claim that I had not given a statement to the Bosnian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: But we determined that this was your signature.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was my first and last name.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Were you signing blank pieces of paper?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Let me say, frankly, this is my first and last name, and I did not say that I had signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So you're saying that this is not your signature.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm just saying this, that I did not give a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Let's not belabour this point. Is this your signature or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: The name, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: My question is: Is that your signature? Is that how you sign your name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I use both the Latin and Cyrillic script to sign.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The Chamber has not had the benefit of seeing Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25 this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yes, I know. I'm aware of that. But I should like to ask the witness to sign his name on a sheet of paper and then we will want to tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will the usher please give this sheet of paper to the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Vucicevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Vucicevic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have a version of the statement that Mr. Petrovic is talking in English. You said you don't have one. If you'd like to take a look.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. That would be helpful, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Will you please sign it several times, three or four times, so that we can really establish how it is that you sign your name. Will you please put two or three of your signatures there. May I now see it? May I see this document, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I should like to tender this into evidence as a Defence Exhibit, but before that, could the usher please show it to you and my learned friends in the Prosecution, if you want to see it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We still haven't seen the statement with the witness' signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just a moment. Yes. We have a copy of the statement in Bosnian. Please give this to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution has available clean copies of all of the statements in English and in B/C/S if those would be helpful for the Chamber rather than copies that may have markings on them from counsel. I'm not sure if we have enough clean copies for everyone, but we certainly seem to have enough clean copies for the Bench. Obviously these statements have not yet been translated into French. We can certainly endeavour to do that. The case manager informed me that there are approximately 22 pages in total of these statements and that that would require approximately three to four days for the Translation Unit to translate them into French, but I can certainly make copies into English and the B/C/S versions available right now if that would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. And in principle, counsel should have ready and at hand available copies for the Bench if this is not to be a private exercise between counsel and the witness. We have to assess the evidence, and if you want us to look at the handwriting, then we have to see the two documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, please receive my apologies. I fully accept the criticism, but we did not know that the witness would deny that he had signed this statement. Now, will the Prosecutor now give you a copy in B/C/S which you can have or do you want this copy that I have? Which one of the two would you prefer, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In order to expedite the procedure, you will be tendering those, I take it, as exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: They can be tendered and they can be passed up to us later, and you can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do not think I will be able to conclude my cross-examination by the end of our today's session so that I will prepare everything that you have just instructed me to prepare by tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness H, do you know somebody called Dusan Stamenic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Where did this man live?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was in the same village that I lived in during my detention in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. Just a moment, because the Chamber is conferring.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that mister -- that during the war, Mr. Stamenic, and there I interrupted you. Could you please tell us what you wanted to say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: But can you repeat that question?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I asked you if you knew him. You said you did. What else do you know about him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he wore -- yes, police, village police. He wore a uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Would you relate some incidents to him? Do you remember anything?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. He and many other men came there, especially when those bodies were buried. They were my neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So you remember him from that occasion when the bodies were buried. Do you remember him by something else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, from the camps, because he came to the camps.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did he ever slap anybody in the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were such instances too.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did he do anything else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A man was shot near his home, too. I don't know how. But there was a man who was killed next to -- by his house.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Who killed that man?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it happened next to his house.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So you don't know who killed that man? All you know is that it happened next to his house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
