utterances.text: I know that that same man came for me to bury those bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I got that. What I'm asking is about that murder that you are mentioning which happened near his house. All you know is that it happened near his house; didn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was not an eye witness, I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Then why did you, in your statement, say that on the 20th of August, 1992, Dusan Stamenic fired a rifle and killed an unknown Bosniak?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, those are two different men, sir. Dusan Stamenic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And who?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: And as you said, his son.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I think my question was clear, and I was asking you about Dusan Stamenic. I never asked you about his son and whether if anything his son did?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: The murder happened near the house of Dusan and Drasko Stamenic, near the railway tracks, and near Bektasevic whom the gentleman forced to bury him buried him. Stamanics forced him to bury him.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Why did you say in a statement that "Dusan Stamenic killed a Bosniak whom I did not know"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it says that he killed, he came and forced the man, but I never said that I saw him kill that man.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: That man was buried, you said, by Bektasevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Meaz.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Why, then, did you say in that statement that you, your nephew, Samir Hodzic and Bektasevic buried this man?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because this self same Bektasevic buried that man because he was buried very shallowly. We once went into that meadow and dogs or something had already started, you know -- they had dug him out, and it reeked of -- there were those odours. And Mr. Stamenic was present there on that occasion, and he forced us to bury him.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I suppose the second time you buried him in the cemetery which was near your house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Where did you bury him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: That man is buried next to the fish pond, not far from Dusan and Drasko Stamenic's house, about 300 or 400 metres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness H, could you please slow down? Because it is my impression that the interpreters can get every second or third word because you are just too fast. Will you please try to slow down because the interpreters have to keep up with you and we need to make their work easier. So if I understand you well, you buried that man for the second time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Both times you buried him?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Let me rephrase this. Did you see that body? Did you really see that body?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: His legs could be seen and he had some shoes on and had some working clothes, and it -- the stench was horrible. Nobody would really be happy to see such a person.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you identify that working clothes that you said he had on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, well, overalls.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Then why did you in your statement of the 3rd of November, 1994, did you say that the man had blue jeans, ordinary shoes, a sort of white coffee jacket and a blue shirt?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have just said, it was a kind of a coverall. Perhaps it was jeans. And I said that there was a very unpleasant odour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And that jacket and shirt, do they really look like overalls or like working clothes? Is that how you see it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because I said then, as I'm telling you, that he had a kind of workman's shoes, perhaps these overalls, perhaps it could have been jeans, because as we know, there are overalls and overalls, they come in all colours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Would you wear a jacket with such overalls?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how you put these two together. I just said that these overalls could be just the same colour as the jacket or the shirt, a two-piece.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And what colour were those overalls?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have already said, the lower part was blue. The body had already been buried and it stank and the dogs had already --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mundis?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Objection on relevance grounds, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise but this question goes to the credibility of the witness and I hope you will allow me to continue. I will try to be as brief and concise but you see how the witness answers. I mean, the witness is answering questions that were not asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Inaudible]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Credibility of the witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just deal with it very quickly, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know of a man called had Himzo Hrnic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us what happened to that man?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: That man died. He was starved to death or died as a result of beating in the camp. I buried him in that cemetery next to my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: If one is to judge by the statement that you gave to the investigators in January, 1995, on the 10th of June, 1992, you and some others buried Himzo Hrnic in those four plastic bags; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not. What I stated is that in the cemetery next to my house, of those four men who were brought in plastic bags, I buried both Himzo Hrnic and Safet Kararic and Muranovic and I can't remember his first name. One of those men.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So it was on the 10th of June, 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. On the 10th of June, I buried four men who were brought from the Trnopolje camp. And those other men, I went to bury after I returned from the camp at Trnopolje, from Keraterm to Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When did this man come?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Simply at the same time when I did, when the Keraterm was disbanded, and he died in -- at the Trnopolje in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, do you know somebody called Ermin Hodzic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did Ermin -- was Ermin Hodzic killed on the day when Zoran Karlica's Intervention Platoon came on the 9th of July?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In your statement, you said that that body was buried, that that man was killed, and that his body was buried 20 days later?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Now, let me go back to this 9th of June. You say that those members of the unit, which was called Zoran Karlica, had some patches. What did these patches look like?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the first time I saw it. It was round and it said "Zoran Karlica Intervention Platoon." I know what it was like but I can't exactly tell you, but it has a drawing but I don't know --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And what colour --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. It was round and I think it had white lettering saying "Intervention Platoon, Zoran Karlica."

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You said that every five to ten days or so, a street in Trnopolje would be evicted. Will you now try to remember the sequence, as I suppose you are familiar with all the streets? Could you tell us something about the sequence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you. I know that on the 9th of July, the evicted were Matrici, Duracici, Muranovici, Elezi, and my street. And I cannot tell you the exact dates for all the streets because my village is large. It is one of the largest villages in the Prijedor municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I wasn't asking you about the date. I'm asking you about the names.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Five or ten days before the 9th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Which street was evicted?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you exactly. Perhaps it was first Elezi, then Karlici and then Sesta. I can't really tell you for sure because it was a long time ago, the exact date or the sequence or the days, five or ten.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Were there any armed men in Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my knowledge, as I have already said, I do not belong to any political party. It is, of course, possible that there were, and the Territorial Defence, but I wasn't interested in politics.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And where were those armed men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say that because I wasn't in any one of those units, as I have already said.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: But did you leave your house ever?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: My house? Well, that street and that whole place was practically a camp. Yes, I could move about, but at my own responsibility, risking to be killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I'm trying to get an answer from you, and that is if there were any armed guards in Trnopolje and if you saw them.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why, there was the Territorial Defence, naturally. There was those in the Territorial Defence before the beginning of the conflict, mutually. They were the -- people went on duty, and it was distributed between Muslims, Croats, Ukrainians, and Serbs. But that there were some formations that carried weapons, I mean Muslims, but I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what a Crisis Staff is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why, yes. Well, this thing before the war in the Territorial Defence, yes, we had it in our Territorial Defence in Trnopolje. We had those kind of a Crisis Staff, the TO, before the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And what was the role of that Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's the Territorial Defence, and it was supposed to protect regardless of the population, Muslim, Serb, in case of a conflict, but we saw what happened and how it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Were the members of the Territorial Defence armed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the Territorial Defence, they were armed before by those self-same authorities, by the police and the municipality authority that issued those men with weapons. And I cannot tell you about this because I was not in any one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When you left your homes, how many men did you say walked down the street towards Trnopolje, towards the centre?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: Down that street of mine to the asphalt road which runs across the field, that is Prijedor-Omarska. And my street was 800 to 1.000 metres long and there were some 60 to 70 elderly male persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And how many people perished?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G [Resumed]
utterances.text: From my street, 26 people were killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, if this is a convenient time, we would take the break until tomorrow morning, because the Chamber does have to prepare itself for another matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Yes, we shall continue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I ask you to have ready tomorrow morning those documents that were tendered. There was some lack of clarity. The documents that were tendered by Mr. Petrovic, various statements, and the document with the signature of the witness for tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Mr. Vucicevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may address the Court on a technical matter. I do not have access to the laptop as the Prosecutor does and the other counsel do, and it just happened the way we took the seating, according to the name that you are calling, the counsel here, and I have brought this matter to the attention of the Registry when I -- when we started the trial, and it's been two and a half weeks, and I really don't have a computer to mark anything on the transcript and perhaps to go back. I know if I have -- like I will have opportunity for this witness, I can, you know, down-load it and look it up, but if I had to examine this witness, I wouldn't have any way to look at his testimony, what he had done earlier. So I contacted the technical people, and they said ask the Registry or ask Trial Chamber to give me permission to have another line access to the LiveNote. I'm at disadvantage and doctrine of equity of arms, I believe, gives me a chance to be in equal position of all other counsel. Can I have my own laptop too? I brought my own in. Just the line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The Chamber will investigate this matter. I think you have every right to the use of the same technical equipment as other counsel, and we'll discuss this with the Registrar and the other appropriate authorities. Witness H, we're going to adjourn now until tomorrow morning at 9.30. During the adjournment, you're reminded that you're not to discuss your evidence with anybody, including members of the Prosecution team. We are adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 5th day of April, 2001, at 9.30 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 4.00 p.m.,
